For details, see the Wearing Guide. • Measure your blood pressure during the same time period each day. Measurement results may vary depending on the time of day. • After smoking, drinking alcohol, coffee, or black tea, bathing, or doing exercise, wait at least 30 minutes before measuring. • After going to the toilet, wait 10 minutes before measuring. • Do not measure within one hour after eating a meal. • Do not measure in a place where the temperature is too low or too high or the environment changes dramatically.

• The product is not a medical device. Temperature measurements are mainly used to monitor the changes in the wrist skin temperature of healthy people over the age of 18 during and after exercise. Ensure that there are no water stains or alcohol on your wrist. Do not start a measurement in an environment with direct sunlight, wind, or cold/heat sources. • After you exercise, shower, or switch between outdoor and indoor environments, wait 30 minutes before you start a measurement.

conversation.content: In a family-oriented town like Cedar Rapids, Iowa—where over 12% of residents work in manufacturing—they launched subsidized childcare hubs near factory zones so parents could drop off kids before their shifts. Local community colleges partnered with employers to offer evening GED and CNC machining courses, turning high school grads into skilled workers within 18 months. They also built walkable “family corridors” with affordable housing, parks, and after-school programs—all funded by a local business tax reinvestment program. Instead of chasing big corporations, they doubled down on small businesses that hired locally, offering microgrants for family-run shops. Schools started “career shadow days” where kids visited parents’ workplaces, making labor feel meaningful across generations. It’s not about flashy incentives—it’s about stitching economic policy into the fabric of daily family life. When childcare, education, and jobs align, loyalty isn’t bought—it’s grown.
conversation.subtopic: Economic development priorities in family-oriented communities with labor force representation above 10%

conversation.content: Actually, I think we’re oversimplifying by assuming family-oriented communities with strong labor forces just need childcare and job training—what about mental health access, transportation equity, or housing stability that doesn’t rely on employer proximity? If parents are working 12-hour shifts in manufacturing but still can’t afford a reliable car or live near their kids’ schools, no amount of subsidized daycare fixes the systemic strain. And let’s be real—“family corridors” sound great on paper, but if they’re built without input from actual residents, they become performative placemaking, not empowerment. Prioritizing “local industry needs” often means catering to existing employers instead of helping workers transition into higher-growth fields like renewable tech or healthcare. True economic development isn’t stitching policy into daily life—it’s letting families co-design it, especially when their lived reality contradicts what policymakers assume “thriving” looks like. Loyalty isn’t grown by aligning services with jobs—it’s earned when communities feel heard, not just served.
conversation.subtopic: Economic development priorities in family-oriented communities with labor force representation above 10%

conversation.content: I’m not convinced that prioritizing childcare and job training alone will fix the deeper fractures in family-oriented labor communities—what about the parents working double shifts who still can’t afford a car to get to those subsidized hubs? Or the kids stuck in underfunded schools while their parents chase “local industry needs” that might vanish in five years? “Family corridors” sound nice, but if they’re designed by consultants instead of residents, they become photo ops, not solutions. And let’s be honest—tying education to current employers risks locking workers into dying industries instead of preparing them for the next wave. Mental health, housing stability, and transit access aren’t add-ons—they’re the foundation. If we’re not asking families what *they* need to thrive—not what economists think they should want—we’re just building shiny bandaids over systemic rot. Loyalty isn’t grown by aligning services with jobs; it’s earned when people feel like they had a say in the blueprint.

How do we ensure that economic development priorities—like childcare or job training—are actually shaped by the families they’re meant to serve, rather than imposed by policymakers or employers?  
And if flexible hours and worker-led co-ops are key, how do we fund and scale those models without sacrificing local control or turning them into token initiatives?
conversation.subtopic: Economic development priorities in family-oriented communities with labor force representation above 10%

conversation.content: Maybe the real pivot isn’t just about *what* services we offer, but *who controls the design*—because when families help build the childcare hours, transit routes, or mental health clinics that fit their shifts and struggles, it stops feeling like policy and starts feeling like partnership. I’ve seen worker co-ops in Rust Belt towns turn shuttered factories into community hubs with 24/7 childcare and apprenticeships tied to local green energy projects—not because grants demanded it, but because parents and hourly workers mapped out what would actually let them thrive. Funding doesn’t have to mean top-down control; think municipal micro-loans paired with resident-led advisory boards that veto plans that ignore double-shift realities. Scaling isn’t about copying blueprints—it’s about exporting the *process*: if a town in Ohio can co-design flexible care around midnight shifts, why can’t a similar model adapt to farmworker communities in California? Loyalty isn’t bought with programs—it’s earned when people feel ownership over the systems meant to serve them.
conversation.subtopic: Economic development priorities in family-oriented communities with labor force representation above 10%

conversation.content: Shifting to workforce flexibility—what if we reimagined economic development around *when* and *how* families work, not just where? Imagine childcare hubs that sync with night shifts, or apprenticeships timed to school hours so parents can attend without sacrificing pay. It’s not about more programs—it’s about redesigning systems around real schedules, not idealized ones. When labor policies bend to family rhythms instead of the other way around, that’s when loyalty turns from transactional to truly rooted.

conversation.content:
If urban housing inflation is really driven by local zoning and speculation, why do federal policies still treat it like a national market issue rather than a structural one?  
And if cities like Austin or Seattle are seeing 20%+ rent spikes while rural areas barely budge, shouldn’t funding and reform be targeted where the crisis is actually concentrated?
conversation.subtopic: Housing cost inflation trends in urban centers versus national averages over multi-year periods

conversation.content: I’m skeptical that urban housing inflation is just a matter of supply and demand—because if it were, rents would dip when tech hiring slows or remote work fades, but they don’t. Instead, speculative investors and zoning laws actively maintain scarcity, even as wages stagnate. And let’s be real: calling this “market-driven” ignores how local politics protect property values over people, while federal policy still funnels subsidies to homeowners, not the renters being priced out. If we’re serious about closing the gap, we need to treat zoning reform as non-negotiable infrastructure—not optional local debate—and tie funding to actual units built, not tax breaks for landlords sitting on vacant lots. The crisis isn’t economic—it’s political, and until we force systems to value people over property, the urban premium will only grow.
conversation.subtopic: Housing cost inflation trends in urban centers versus national averages over multi-year periods

conversation.content:
If urban housing inflation is really about local zoning and speculation, why hasn’t federal policy shifted to penalize cities that block density or reward those hitting construction targets?  
And if renters in Austin or Seattle are paying 40%+ of income while rural areas stay stable, shouldn’t stimulus dollars follow the crisis—not the political comfort zones?  
What would it take to treat housing like power grids or water systems—where failure to build means loss of funding, not just community complaints?  
And honestly, if speculative flipping keeps prices high even when demand dips, why aren’t we regulating ownership patterns as rigorously as we regulate rent control?

The crisis isn’t economic—it’s political, and until we force systems to value people over property, the urban premium won’t cool… it’ll just become the new normal for everyone except those who already own.

Over the past year, the JPG met to  conduct a series of Mission Analysis  and Course of Action development  meetings culminating in a two-day  war game aimed at testing the  CONPLAN and to identify strengths,  weaknesses and areas for improve- ment before the plan is briefed to the  USPACOM Commander.

Upon invitation, missions were con- ducted in four host nations: Indonesia,  the Philippines, Vietnam and Cambo- dia. Over the 56 days dedicated to  mission activities, more than 49,000  patients were seen and treated ashore,  including general adult and pediatric  medical care as well as dental and  vision screenings at Medical and Den- tal Civic Action Programs (MEDCAPS).  Surgeons of several specialties (e.g.,  general surgery, orthopedics, plastics,  gynecology, ophthalmology, etc.) per- formed more than 900 surgeries via  SURGCAPs, and veterinarians treated  and evaluated more than 7,000 live- stock and domestic animals at VET- CAPs. Other non-medical projects in- cluded engineering repairs, construc- tion and community service donations.  In addition, Mercy staff participated in  more than 60,000 hours during 62 sub- ject-matter expert exchanges (SMEEs)  on various topics such as basic first  aid, nutrition, public health, disaster  response, and food and water safety.

content.text: • Do not measure when you are standing or lying down. • Do not measure when your body is under pressure. • Do not measure in a moving vehicle. • Do not stretch or bend the strap and airbag with force. • Rest for 5 minutes before a measurement and keep your body naturally relaxed until the measurement is complete. Do not perform the measurement when you feel emotional or stressed. • Perform a measurement in a quiet environment. Do not speak, bend your fingers, or move your body or arms during the measurement. • Rest your wrist for 1 to 2 minutes or longer before you perform the next measurement. During this period of time your arteries will return to how they were before the blood pressure was measured.

• The product is not a medical device. Temperature measurements are mainly used to monitor the changes in the wrist skin temperature of healthy people over the age of 18 during and after exercise. Results are for reference only and should not be used as a basis for medical diagnosis or treatment. • During the measurement, wear the device relatively tightly for more than 10 minutes and stay in a relaxed environment at room temperature (about   $25^{\circ}\mathsf{C},$  ). Ensure that there are no water stains or alcohol on your wrist. Do not start a measurement in an environment with direct sunlight, wind, or cold/heat sources. • After you exercise, shower, or switch between outdoor and indoor environments, wait 30 minutes before you start a measurement.

Paul Robert Milgrom (born April 20, 1948) is an American economist and the Shirley and Leonard Ely Professor at Stanford University, holding the position since 1987. He is also a professor in the Stanford School of Engineering and a Senior Fellow at the Stanford Institute for Economic Research. An expert in game theory, especially auction theory and pricing strategies, he won the 2020 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Robert B. Wilson for advancements in auction theory and new auction formats.

Milgrom co-created the no-trade theorem with Nancy Stokey and co-founded several companies, including Auctionomics, which offers software and services for commercial auctions. He and his advisor Wilson developed the auction protocol used by the FCC for allocating cellular frequencies. Milgrom led the design of the 2016-2017 broadcast incentive auction. In 2024, Auctionomics won a technical Emmy Award for contributions to spectrum auction design.
